date: 2026-10-08: Core ML or Core AI for the learned disk detector
lede: One question, parked by you on 2026-09-23 to be re-decided later. A draft sheet and an independent second opinion both checked Apple's documentation through the docs MCP; both recommend staying on Core ML and deciding by a short measured spike.

cards.title: Core ML or Core AI for the learned disk detector
context: The learned disk detector (a 256 px U-Net) runs on the Neural Engine through Core ML. On the M5 Pro, Core ML's automatic setting ran it on the GPU, and the Neural Engine served only one batch size; the app now checks at load that the Neural Engine really ran it and refuses otherwise. Why the scheduler behaves that way is not established.

Apple's Core AI framework (macOS 27) can run the same kind of model and documents a way to prefer the Neural Engine. But its pages for that targeting list iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, visionOS and watchOS — not macOS — and the option is only a preference, not a guarantee. Core ML's `.cpuAndNeuralEngine` is already an explicit request, and the app already verifies placement.
Your in-app fine-tuning writes a Core ML package; Core AI has no on-device writer, so moving fully to Core AI would drop or split that path.

Code this unlocks: a — nothing now, a spike later (about one session). b — port the runtime (about 110 lines exist in history), a PyTorch export, and a Gate D because the numbers move (3–4 sessions). c — both behind one protocol (4–5 sessions) and twice the held-out validation.

glossary.meaning: Apple's on-chip accelerator for neural networks; fast and power-efficient for inference.
a short, time-boxed measurement to settle a question before committing to a change.
the number of patterns run at once; the only size the Neural Engine served on the M5.

cards.question: Stay on Core ML, move to Core AI, or support both?

options.label: Stay on Core ML; run a spike at the next detector change
options.what: Nothing changes now. The spike first checks Core AI's macOS availability and Neural Engine placement for one pattern; only if Core AI wins on placement, speed and detection parity (batch 32, same weights, scan-level peaks) is the runtime reopened.
options.effort: 0 now; about 1 session for the spike
options.risk: low; the Core ML workaround stays until then

options.label: Move the bundled detector to Core AI
options.what: Core AI's tools and a preferred-Neural-Engine setting; fine-tuned models would still need Core ML.
options.risk: high: new framework, macOS targeting undocumented, numbers move

options.label: Both runtimes behind one protocol
options.what: Choose per model; compare side by side during a migration.
options.risk: highest upkeep; every backend needs its own held-out validation (ADR 043)

cards.recommendWhy: Core ML already requests and verifies the Neural Engine; Core AI's advantage is undocumented on macOS and its targeting is only a preference. A spike settles it cheaply when the detector next changes.
cards.advisor: Agrees with a, on corrected grounds: Core AI's preferredComputeUnitKind is not a stronger guarantee than Core ML's explicit request plus the app's load check, and Core AI's model pages list no macOS availability. The spike must start with that availability check and a one-pattern placement probe, compare at batch 32 with placement confirmed in both runtimes, keep the same weights, and judge scan-level peaks — or a silent fallback would look like parity. Not c: two runtimes double the held-out work.
cards.nothing: a — Core ML stays, the spike waits for the next detector change.

not_carded: Answered on 2026-10-07 night (ADR 061): V5-8 = b; P2 keep 320; P4 = b; P1, P3, P5 confirmed.
Swift 6 (64 diagnostics, 3.5–5 sessions) is a scheduling question for you, not a card: say when you want it.
